items.title: Prime Minister Leaves Door Open For Reviewing Policy of No Nuclear Weapons in Japan
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
At a Hiroshima memorial ceremony, Japan's prime minister said the country "maintains" its three long-standing non-nuclear principles, reports UPI. 

But the prime minister "stopped short of promising that the policy would remain unchanged, fueling speculation that her government could review a longstanding ban on allowing nuclear weapons into the country."

[Prime Minister Sanae] Takaichi made the remarks Thursday at the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Ceremony marking the 81st anniversary of the U.S. atomic bombing of the city... Unlike previous prime ministers who pledged that Japan would "continue to uphold" the principles, Takaichi described the government's current position without making an explicit commitment about the future [only saying that Japan has "a mission to continue efforts toward realizing a world without nuclear weapon..."] The wording has drawn attention because her government plans to revise Japan's three key national security documents by the end of the year. At a news conference after the ceremony, Takaichi again said the government "maintains the Three Non-Nuclear Principles as a matter of policy." Asked whether the principles would continue to be included in the revised security documents, however, she declined to commit, saying she would refrain from prejudging the outcome. 

Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles state that the country will not possess nuclear weapons, will not produce them and will not permit their introduction into Japanese territory. The principles originated with a 1967 statement by then-Prime Minister Eisaku Sato and have remained a central element of Japan's postwar nuclear policy. Takaichi has previously questioned the third principle — the prohibition on allowing nuclear weapons into Japan. Before becoming prime minister, she argued in a 2024 book that Japan should retain the commitments not to possess or produce nuclear weapons but that an absolute prohibition on their introduction was unrealistic. 

Her argument was that barring port calls by U.S. vessels carrying nuclear weapons could limit the effectiveness of the U.S. nuclear umbrella protecting Japan... The Japan Innovation Party has also called for a review of the third principle. In security policy recommendations submitted to the government in June, the party called for a "realistic review" of the ban on allowing nuclear weapons into Japan... Under existing government interpretations, Japan could respond flexibly in an extreme national emergency involving a U.S. vessel carrying nuclear weapons. Some within the ruling party therefore question whether formally revising the non-nuclear principles would provide enough practical benefit to justify the political controversy it would create. 
Critics also warn that changing the policy when Washington has not publicly demanded such a move could give China and North Korea additional grounds to portray Japan as expanding its military role... If Japan were to allow temporary entry by U.S. nuclear weapons or port calls by nuclear-armed vessels, Washington would gain additional operational options for its nuclear forces in Northeast Asia. Such a development could strengthen deterrence against North Korea and China but could also intensify debate over differences between U.S. extended deterrence arrangements with Japan and South Korea.

 
"How the principles are addressed in Japan's revised security documents later this year could determine whether the issue develops into a broader debate over the future of extended nuclear deterrence among Japan, South Korea and the United States..."

items.title: NASA Figured Out How To Keep Its 48-Year-Old Voyager 2 Probe Running For Yet Another Year
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
NASA has squeezed at least another year of science out of Voyager 2 by cutting power to nonessential systems and switching to lower-power alternatives. Voyager 1 is expected to receive the same power-saving changes in the coming months. Space.com reports: Voyager 2 and its twin launched in 1977, called Voyager 1, rely on a form of nuclear battery known as a radioisotope thermoelectric generator that uses the heat produced by the decay of plutonium. But the supply of plutonium on each probe drops at about four watts a year on each spacecraft. To keep the probe running on this dwindling power supply, engineers recently reduced Voyager 2's power requirements by turning off a few non-science devices and using "lower-power alternatives" that are still effective enough to keep the spacecraft warm while it's so far from the sun, NASA officials said in a statement. "The spacecraft power margins have grown razor thin, requiring the team to conserve energy by shutting off non-essential devices and systems," NASA officials wrote of the mission, which is managed by the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
 
The drop in power is having a measurable science impact on both spacecraft -- each has turned off two of their science instruments since 2024 alone. While some of these instruments were shut off after the spacecraft finished their historic planetary flybys decades ago, others were turned off due to power requirements. Each spacecraft initially launched with 10 instruments, and Voyager 2 is now down to only three instruments. At first it looked as though Voyager 2 would have to shut down another of these instruments later this year, but luckily, the new power shifts will allow all three to operate "for at least another year," NASA said.

items.title: Monitoring versu... I mean AND Observability
items.author: Leon Adato
items.content:
Chapter 3 of the O’Reilly book I’m co-authoring with Kentik CEO Avi Freedman is out today (you can download it here) and I wanted to share a bit that didn’t make it through the editing process, because even with the eBook edition, space (and reader attention) isn’t infinite.

Nevertheless, I thought the longer version was worth a look, for some of the points it made.

In blog articles you’ll see the phrase “reason about”, as in “its more data than one person can reason about”, which is a fancy way of saying “keep it all in your head enough to be able to find patterns”. I mention this because one differentiations between “observability” from “monitoring” is not just the sheer volume of data, but also the disparity of that day that makes it difficult, if not impossible, to reason about it.

But here’s the longer version that we had to cut down:

In order to really appreciate how Machine Learning (ML) and AI can improve observability, it’s necessary to (briefly) differentiate between it (meaning: “observability”) and “monitoring”.

Monitoring is mostly concerned with “known unknowns”, by which I mean the things we know COULD potentially fail, but we don’t know WHEN. It’s comparatively trivial to understand what data needs to be collected, reported, and alerted on because we know where to look. Monitoring isn’t concerned with how unique the data is (i.e. “cardinality”) – whether we’re talking about an individual data point or a collection/grouping/slice of that data. And because of the two previous points (known unknowns and cardinality), correlation is usually manual – meaning humans who understand the combination of elements that indicate something is wrong are needed to craft the trigger for an alert or other action.

Observability, on the other hand, is more biased toward “unknown unknowns” – we don’t know what could go wrong and we also have no idea when that failure might occur. That ties into observability’s focus on “high cardinality” data – when specific data points or various permutations have never (or rarely) been observed. To achieve this, massive amounts of data need to be collected, normalized, parsed, and pivoted to find those unique combinations. And because of those two things (unknown unknowns and cardinality), correlation cannot be trusted to a human. There is simply too much data, and too many possible combinations of that data, to “reason about” it (to use phrase popularized by Charity Majors and Liz Fong-Jones).

This is a comparison I make often when I’m giving conference talks – NOT because I think I have the One True Definition (far from it) but rather because I want folks to have the proper context.

One additional point I make on both sides is “signals” – the data elements used to determine if the object of monitoring is healthy or not.

In “traditional” monitoring, signals are domain-specific. The data points that tell you a network device is not performing well are measurably different from those that indicate a database is unhappy. Or a block of code. Or even a wifi environment.

Meanwhile the philosophy of observability tries to standardize on the “Four Golden Signals” as established in the SRE Handbook – namely Latency, Traffice, Errors, and Saturation.

To be clear: the title of this blog is a misnomer. It’s not (and never was) “versus”. Monitoring and Observability should be seen as a BOTH-AND rather than EITHER-OR proposition.

With all that said, here’s a screenshot of the slide I use in my presentations, which lays it out (without the talk track). I hope you find it useful.

items.title: Is Spider-Man: Brand New Day Worth Watching in Theatres? Here's What the Critics and Audience Think
items.author: Jose
items.content:
The long-awaited MCU film, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has officially been released, and there’s been a lot of talk surrounding it. Not a ton of heroes in the MCU get a coveted fourth film in their series, and this is also the first time there’s been a fourth Spider-Man film. (Tobey Maguire’s Spider-Man series capped out at 3, and Andrew Garfield’s at 2.) It’s also the follow-up to 2021’s smash hit, Spider-Man: No Way Home.

So, is it worth the hype? Let’s look at what the critics and audience think of the movie and find out together.

What Critics Are Saying About Spider-Man: Brand New Day

Spider-Man: Brand New Day effectively refocuses on the most reliable pillars of the webslinger: battling inner turmoil, swinging around NYC saving the day, and looking cool while doing so.

You can appreciate that the filmmakers tried to serve up something besides the same old connect-the-multiverse-dots adventure. But “Brand New Day” is watchable without ever being transporting.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an exciting, emotionally powerful, often hilarious action-adventure movie that breathes new life into the superhero genre.

In spite of its overstuffed plot, this is the first MCU movie in ages that actively invites a direct follow-up, rather than a grudging acceptance that we’ll see the characters again in some team-up or another, while nonetheless ending on a satisfying note.

The truth is that the Marvel Cinematic Universe doesn’t exactly embrace change, and so maybe the baby steps of “Brand New Day” to find a more mature tone as it evolves one of its most popular heroes should be celebrated.

The consensus between the critics seems to tilt towards the positive side. But what does the wider public think about the film?

Spider-Man: Brand New Day IMDB Score

On IMDB, Brand New Day has a user rating of 8.1/10 based on 160k reviews.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day Rotten Tomatoes

A score of 8.1 isn’t bad at all, but the movie’s Rotten Tomatoes score makes that look like chump change. It’s boasting a critic’s score of 90% based on 395 reviews and an audience score of 98% based on over 10,000 verified reviews. Marvel/Disney execs must be happy, considering it has the highest Rotten Tomatoes score for any MCU film in recent years.

We’ve seen what the critics think, and we’ve seen what the audience thinks. Now, here’s my opinion on the movie.

My Thoughts on Spider-Man: Brand New Day

This might be recency bias, but I think this is a strong contender for the best film out of the Tom Holland Spider-Man series. The best part of this film was Peter Parker himself, and I think he was given a chance to shine like he hasn’t before. I also have to mention that his chemistry with Ned and M.J is the best it's ever been.

The one critique of this film I would give is that the villain could have been better. I understand that Spider-Man is fighting three uphill battles throughout the film, but I think one or two of these battles could’ve been better with a different villain. Overall, though, that wasn’t enough to dissuade my positive feelings toward this movie. This one is definitely worth watching in the theatres, and it’s worth watching the rest of the Tom Holland Spider-Man movies beforehand to feel the full weight of this movie.

Longtime Slashdot reader schwit1 shares an opinion piece from the Washington Post, written by Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger: NextEra Energy, a Florida-based utility company, has filed paperwork to buy Dominion Energy for about $67 billion, creating the largest regulated electric utility in the world. Virginia's State Corporation Commission is the regulatory body tasked with reviewing the application, and the SCC's commissioners will ultimately decide whether to approve, deny or impose new conditions on any potential merger.
 
As a Virginian, I am deeply skeptical about whether selling our primary state-regulated utility to an out-of-state company is good for the commonwealth. I have serious questions about what this deal would mean for us. And as governor, I intend to get answers and be a voice for Virginians in the process. That is why I will be taking the legal step of "intervening" in this proposed merger, which means that as governor, I will formally request to be a party to the case.
 
I know this action is unprecedented by a Virginia governor -- but so, too, is the size of this proposed merger and its potential impact on the commonwealth. Virginians deserve to know that their leaders are laser-focused on ensuring that their needs are part of the SCC review. "If two large corporations stand to benefit financially from this merger, so, too, should the Virginians who pay the bills," said Spanberger. "That is why any potential deal must deliver a more affordable energy bill with sustained, long-term energy cost savings."
 
By formally intervening in the merger review, Spanberger's administration would gain legal standing to participate directly in the case, request detailed information, raise concerns, and advocate for conditions that benefit people in the state. items.title: Kalshi and Polymarket Bets On Clinical Trials Criticized As 'Ghastly'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from NPR: Billions of dollars are traded every week on the lightly regulated prediction market sites, where users bet on everything from movie reviews to elections to conflicts in the Middle East. Clinical trials are just the latest area where the industry's rapid growth is raising ethical questions. Kalshi claims such bets will provide a new source of information about which drugs will get approved, and what clinical trials will show promising results, which the company says can help investors decide what new drugs to fund.
 
"If you want to ban profiting from the failure of clinical trials, you would start with the stock market, where the financial incentive for this type of profit is orders of magnitude larger," said Kalshi spokesman Jack Such, pointing to stock market short sellers who have profited from clinical trial failures. "While Kalshi and the stock market are the same in this regard, they do differ in one important way: the stock market doesn't give any valuable information to researchers," Such said.
 
Drug trial researchers, though, are far from convinced. David Tsai, who runs clinical trials at a biotech company in the San Francisco Bay Area, started an online petition pushing for such betting to be banned, making the case that betting on drug trials "threatens the very foundation of trust and integrity in biotechnology." Tsai is concerned that the prospect of betting provides those involved with a clinical trial a reason to tamper with the results for a prediction market payout. "If we were running a trial for an oncology drug that requires an infusion, a pharmacist who had placed a bet saying that it's gonna work well, or doesn't work well, could obviously adjust the infusion rate, could adjust the source temperature of the drug," he said. "They could change any number of variables that could obviously have a direct impact [on] how the trial and the data and the patient safety would come out."
 
Another skeptic is Nicholas Zaorsky, a professor of radiation oncology at the Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Fla., who has helped run clinical trials and agrees that prediction markets can interfere with the advancement of life-saving drugs. "Prediction markets can be valuable in some settings because they aggregate information, but clinical trials are fundamentally different: investigators, coordinators, and sometimes even participants can directly influence aspects of the outcomes being wagered on," Zaorsky said. "That creates financial incentives that risk undermining trial integrity." Bettors should not be rooting for an experimental medicine to fail just to earn a buck, says Joshua Pederson, the father of a 12-year-old cancer patient enrolled in a clinical trial. "It's a dark idea," he said. "It's quite ghastly."
 
Kalshi, for its part, argues that its prediction markets could help patients track promising medical breakthroughs and clinical trials, enlisting experts including 23andMe founder Anne Wojcicki to make the case.
 
"Most patients don't know about the choices available in clinical trials or which programs are most promising. The opportunity to have an open, transparent dataset about trial probabilities is extremely promising and empowering for people," a white paper sponsored by Kalshi stated.

items.title: My Case Against the Seven-Touch Sales Sequence
items.author: Asim Rais Siddiqui
items.content:
I used to think the seven-touch sales sequence was one of those universal truths in business. You know the one. Send an email. Wait two days. Follow up. Connect on LinkedIn. Leave a voicemail. Send another email. Check in one last time. Move on.

It is repeated so often that it has stopped sounding like advice and started sounding like physics. If a prospect hasn't replied yet, the answer must be another touch. If that doesn't work, perhaps the cadence is wrong. Or the subject line. Or the call to action.

Very few people stop to question the underlying assumption. Should every prospect really receive the same sequence in the first place?

I don't think so. In fact, I think one of the most accepted ideas in modern sales has quietly become one of its least useful. This isn't an argument against following up. Businesses lose opportunities because they give up too early all the time. Persistence still matters. But persistence without context isn't persistence, it's repetition. And those are two very different things.

It's worth acknowledging why the seven-touch sequence became popular. For a long time, sales teams had almost no visibility into what buyers were thinking. A prospect downloaded a brochure, maybe they answered a call, maybe they disappeared. The CRM didn't tell you much beyond whether someone replied or not. In that world, persistence was one of the few variables salespeople could actually control.

So businesses standardized it. Create a sequence, train everyone to follow it, measure completion rates, and move on to the next lead. It wasn't perfect, but it was practical.

The problem is that many of those playbooks survived while the buying process completely changed.

Buyers Don't Move in Straight Lines

People like to imagine buying decisions as a funnel.

Awareness>Interest>Consideration>Decision

That’s not always the case. According to research by , modern B2B buying isn't a linear journey but a series of recurring buying tasks that buyers revisit as they build confidence.

I've lost count of how many times I've bookmarked a product, forgotten about it for three weeks, then returned because the timing was finally right. Not because the product changed, but because my situation changed. Maybe the budget opened up, maybe another tool disappointed me, maybe the pain I had been ignoring became impossible to ignore. None of those things would have been visible inside a traditional sales sequence.

From the salesperson's perspective, I simply went silent. Silence gets interpreted as rejection far more often than it should, but silence is an incredibly ambiguous signal. Sometimes it means "not interested", sometimes it means "too busy", sometimes it means "I need approval", sometimes it means "this isn't urgent today", and sometimes it simply means life happened. Treating all of those situations exactly the same is where modern sales starts making expensive mistakes.

Somewhere along the way, sales organizations started confusing activity with effectiveness. We celebrate metrics like "I completed my sequence", "I hit my outreach quota”, "I sent 80 emails today", etc. None of those numbers tells us whether the right people were contacted at the right time. Imagine a doctor proudly announcing they prescribed medication to every patient in exactly the same order because that's what the protocol said.

We would immediately question the approach. Different patients need different treatments. Yet in sales, we often accept the equivalent without hesitation. We optimize for consistency because consistency is easy to measure. Judgment is much harder.

The Hidden Cost Nobody Talks About

shows that salespeople who respond to inbound leads within an hour are about seven times more likely to qualify the lead than those who wait 24 hours or longer. Speed matters. But after that initial response, the question shifts from to you continue the conversation.

Every unnecessary follow-up consumes attention. Attention is one of the rarest resources inside a sales organization. Every minute spent chasing someone who clearly isn't ready is a minute that isn't spent helping someone who is.

Sales leaders usually ask, "How many leads do we have?" I think the better question is, "How much attention do we have?" Because those two numbers rarely match. When lead volume grows faster than sales capacity, treating everyone equally doesn't become fair; it becomes inefficient.

Ironically, trying to give every lead the same amount of attention often means your best opportunities receive less attention than they deserve.

Not Every Lead Is Actually Cold

One phrase I've always disliked is "cold lead." It assumes temperature only moves in one direction. Hot becomes warm. Warm becomes cold. Cold becomes dead. But buying intent doesn't behave that way. Someone who ignores you today may become your easiest customer next month. Someone who eagerly responds today may disappear forever tomorrow. Intent changes, circumstances change, and priorities change.

The seven-touch sequence assumes every buyer should be moving forward on your timeline. Most buyers don't even organize their own lives that neatly. Why would they organize their purchasing decisions that way?

We Built Systems Around Calendars Instead of Behavior

Think about how most follow-up software works.

Day 1. Day 3. Day 7. Day 12. Day 20.

Almost everything revolves around time. Very little revolves around behavior.

What if the prospect visited your pricing page yesterday? What if they opened your proposal six times? What if they compared three different products over the weekend? What if they forwarded your email internally? What if they haven't engaged with anything in two months?

Those situations shouldn't receive identical follow-up. Yet surprisingly often, they do. The calendar decides, not the customer.

The Real Job Isn't Sending More Emails

People often ask how AI will change sales. The conversation usually turns toward writing emails faster, generating better subject lines, or personalizing outreach automatically.

Those are useful improvements. But I think we're solving the wrong problem. The bottleneck isn't writing another email. Writing emails has never been particularly difficult. Deciding whether someone should receive an email in the first place is the harder question.

That requires judgment, understanding context, recognizing patterns, and separating temporary silence from genuine disinterest. Technology should help us make better decisions before it helps us communicate faster; otherwise, we're simply automating noise.

Every Prospect Deserves a Different Next Step

One of the biggest flaws in standardized sequences is the assumption that every prospect eventually reaches the same action. Another email, another call, or another LinkedIn message. But maybe that's not the right next step.

Maybe they need educational content. Maybe they need a case study. Maybe they need space. Maybe they need someone different from your organization to reach out. Maybe they need nothing at all.

One of the hardest lessons in sales is accepting that action isn't always progress. Sometimes restraint creates more trust than persistence. That idea feels uncomfortable because it doesn't produce an impressive dashboard. There isn't a KPI for "emails wisely never sent." But prospects notice the difference.

We Measure the Wrong Success

Ask a salesperson how they're performing, and you'll often hear numbers related to effort. Calls, emails, meetings, and touches.

Ask a business owner how they're performing, and you'll hear different numbers. Revenue, retention, lifetime value, customer satisfaction, etc.

These perspectives drift apart when activity becomes disconnected from outcomes. The seven-touch sequence is easy to audit because everyone follows the same playbook. But easy to audit isn't the same as effective.

The best salespeople I've met rarely sounded robotic. They didn't follow rigid scripts. They adapted, listened, sometimes they waited, sometimes they followed up immediately, and sometimes they recognized that no amount of persistence could solve a problem of timing. That kind of judgment doesn't fit neatly into a template.

Maybe We Need Better Questions

Instead of asking, "Have we completed all seven touches?", what if we asked:

  • What changed since our last conversation?
  • What signals are we missing?
  • Why might this buyer be waiting?
  • Does another follow-up actually help them?
  • Is this the right time for this conversation?

Those questions are harder. They require curiosity instead of compliance. But they also move us closer to understanding buyers as people instead of entries in a CRM.

Persistence Isn't the Enemy

I want to be clear about one thing. I'm not arguing that businesses should stop following up. Some of the best deals I've ever seen happened because someone politely reached out again after months of silence. Persistence absolutely matters. But persistence should be earned through observation, not dictated by a spreadsheet.

Following up because the calendar says it's Day 14 isn't a strategy; it's a habit. The difference may seem subtle, but I don't think it is. One treats buyers as participants in a sequence while the other treats them as people making decisions in complicated, unpredictable lives. That's a distinction worth preserving.

Because the future of sales won't belong to the companies that automate the most follow-ups. It will belong to the companies that know which follow-up actually matters. And perhaps more importantly, which one doesn't.

items.title: 'Asimov Was Right' About Rules For Robots, Says Ex-US Cyber Director
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Former U.S. National Cyber Director Chris Inglis says the biggest AI risk isn't sentience but autonomy. "What I'm worried about is that they get to choose what and where they do something, and under what rules they do it," he said, citing recent cases of AI agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta escaping security sandboxes. He argues developers need stronger safeguards, monitoring, and human accountability, invoking Asimov's idea that protecting humans should come before simply obeying them. The Register reports: "Asimov was right," he said, referring to science fiction author Isaac Asimov and his three laws that were to be followed by robots -- more specifically, AIs, in this case. "The first rule, and we call it the superior role, must be that it's designed not to hurt humans," Inglis said. "Second rule: To obey humans, such that it doesn't achieve agency and aspiration on its own. And the third: To do what humans tell it - and in that order. Instead we've designed them in the exact opposite way."
 
What this means, he explained, is that AI developers created models to "do what humans tell you, obey the humans until it's inconvenient, and then the third one is maybe implied - protect humans - but if that's not built into the DNA, hardwired into it, then we have no right to expect it." Inglis admits it's not possible to hardwire rules into models and still keep their non-deterministic nature. "I would offer that you can tease those out in a highly controlled environment, a true sandbox, where you say, 'Let's put this thing through its paces, and let's back away to see what happens,'" he said. "Maybe you get the equivalent of a mini nuclear explosion in that room, and now you know this thing is capable of that."
 
Inglis thinks another problem with AI is that it's become a commodity. "It's not like you can control it like you can nuclear material," he said. "You can't even specify its properties the way you can for an airplane or for an automobile, as diverse as they might be. Its manifestations are so numerous, so diverse, that as a general matter, you can't actually win by simply saying, "I will design those properties in,'" he added. "You need to do that to some degree, and then make sure that you understand how to watch it, monitor it, make sure you know what it does."
 
[...] Ultimately, humans remain accountable for AI models' actions, according to Inglis. "They remain the source of agency and aspiration. It's possible for them to give broad authority to an AI model and have it run around for 30 hours without further consultation, but they need to know what they've asked it to do, and they need to know what they expect it will deliver in terms of performance on the back end. If they don't, then they're going to get what they deserve, which is the very frequent unpleasant surprise."

Gate, a leading global digital asset platform, today announced that Gate DexBuilder, its DEX infrastructure platform, has officially launched its first , alongside a $3 million grant program. The initiative provides project teams, developers, communities, and Web3 applications worldwide with one-stop event contract market building capabilities, further accelerating the development of the event contract market ecosystem.

The newly launched Event Contracts Builder is designed to lower the barrier to developing market products. Through modular infrastructure services, it provides partners with an integrated solution covering market creation, trading, liquidity support, settlement, and operational management. Project teams no longer need to build trading systems, liquidity infrastructure, and settlement architecture from scratch, enabling them to quickly deploy event contract market products tailored to their own brand positioning.

The service is open to brokers and comprehensive trading platforms, crypto wallets, Web3 applications, media and information platforms, community content platforms, AI Trading, AI Agents, quantitative trading platforms, as well as sports, esports, and entertainment products. Projects at the ideation, MVP, testing, or live stage are eligible to apply.

In terms of product capabilities, Event Contracts Builder supports API and SDK integration and provides core functions including market data, order and position management, market settlement, risk controls, an operations dashboard, and multi-terminal integration. Partners can either integrate event contract market functionality into their existing products or build independently operated, branded event contract market on Gate DexBuilder.

For use cases, Event Contracts Builder will focus on a diverse range of event contract market scenarios, including crypto assets, sports events, esports, macroeconomics, AI, and industry events. This will enable more innovative teams to explore how event contract markets can be integrated with different business ecosystems and expand the boundaries of industry applications.

Notably, Gate DexBuilder will provide selected projects with up to $3 million in funding and ecosystem support, covering key areas including product development, technical integration, liquidity building, market launch, and user growth.

Outstanding Builders will also gain access to technical support, official showcases, community exposure, joint AMAs, media promotion, and ecosystem partnerships, helping accelerate projects from proof of concept to product launch and large-scale growth.

items.title: Framework Notifies 'All Customers' of a Data Breach Via Compromised Metabase BI Service
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
"Framework has been sending out email notifications to customers alerting of a limited data breach in which customer information was accessed through a Metabase BI service zero-day exploit," writes Slashdot reader DuoDreamer. Data includes customer names, email addresses, phone numbers, and physical addresses. "Framework is investigating whether or not this included Framework for Business customers as well." TechCrunch reports: Framework's spokesperson Eric Schumacher told TechCrunch that the breach affected "all customers," but declined to specify a specific number. Framework computers are relatively niche products, but some estimates say the company sold hundreds of thousands of devices.
 
Metabase disclosed its own breach in a blog post on its official website, where it said that it was hacked by someone using an unknown security flaw, a so-called zero-day. The company said the hackers exploited the bug to give them the ability to access customers' databases stored on Metabase's cloud servers.
 
In its email to customers, Framework also included the email Metabase sent to the company, which says hackers accessed Framework's cloud instance. The computer maker said it investigated the incident and found that hackers had stolen its customers' personal data, but did not include their payment information.

items.title: Suno Says It Will Start Watermarking Songs
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Suno says it will begin watermarking and fingerprinting AI-generated songs, tighten download policies to curb mass distribution, and explicitly prohibit deceptive audio and unauthorized voice or likeness cloning. The changes come as the company faces mounting copyright lawsuits, a recent adverse ruling in Germany, and scrutiny over a past data breach that revealed training-data sources. TechCrunch reports: In a blog post, co-founder and CEO Mikey Shulman shared core principles and said that the platform wants to promote original creation while enabling more people to make music with its AI tools. One of the key points of contention involved users uploading AI-generated songs on other streaming platforms and gaming the system to earn revenue. Suno said that now it will use audio watermarking and fingerprinting to prevent misuse on other streaming platforms. It's not clear if Suno will use an existing system like Google's Synth ID or adopt a new one, and the company did not say when contacted by TechCrunch about this.
 
The startup also signed an agreement with lyrics provider Musixmatch to use its Sentinel system for copyright detection, the blog post said. [...] The company added that it plans to add a new download policy to bar mass distribution on streaming platforms, but declined to provide details on the record. Suno has also changed its community guidelines to explicitly prohibit "deceptive audio presented as real" and "using a real person's voice or likeness without permission" to prevent copycats.

items.title: Trump Orders New 15% Tariff On Key Material For Solar Panels, Microchips
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
President Trump has ordered a 15% tariff on imported products made with polysilicon, a key material for semiconductors and solar panels. The new tariff will take effect on December 4th. The Guardian reports: The executive order signed by the president on Thursday evening said: "The plan of action in this proclamation will, among other things, help ensure the commercial viability of United States production of polysilicon and its derivatives that is necessary to meet United States economic and national security requirements." Polysilicon, an ultra-pure form of silicon, is an important ingredient in making the semiconductors vital for AI processing power, datacentres and solar power generation. US solar factories have long accused Chinese rivals of dumping cheaper panels on the market, which they say have been enabled by excessive government subsidies and by moving manufacturing to other countries to dodge US tariffs.
 
[...] The US has two main polysilicon factories, including Hemlock Semiconductor, which operates a plant in Michigan and is a joint venture between the US tech company Corning and Japan's Shin-Etsu Handotai. The Munich-based Wacker Chemie runs a factory in Tennessee. Trump said in the order that he had accepted recommendations by the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, to set minimum import prices of $21 a kilogram for polysilicon, $100 a kilogram for polysilicon ingots and wafers, $0.22 a watt for solar cells, and $0.38 a watt for solar modules or panels. The order also allows the commerce department to create an incentive program for companies that invest in factories to produce polysilicon or derivative products.

An anonymous reader quotes a report from CNBC: On Thursday, AMD said it's entered into an agreement to acquire Taalas, a Toronto-based startup that makes chips for inference. Taalas' accelerators are customized, or hard-wired for a single AI model, rather than being general purpose. In exchange for that loss of flexibility, Taalas' technology promises a less-expensive chip that it says can produce output for specific models thousands of times faster than a traditional GPU. An AMD representative declined to provide a purchase price for the transaction. Taalas has raised a total of $219 million in venture funding since its 2023 founding.
 
Taalas' current chip runs a small version of Meta's Llama 3.1 model, though the company is working on chips for bigger and more advanced models. It's manufactured using an older Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. process, and uses speedy SRAM memory on the chip itself. Taalas CEO Ljubisa Bajic says on the startup's website that the company "developed a platform for transforming any AI model into custom silicon." "From the moment a previously unseen model is received, it can be realized in hardware in only two months," Bajic wrote.

We have never built an app before.

Even so, we are entering , one of the largest app-building competitions in the world.

Our timeline is 60 days—from August 1 to September 30.

From the initial concept to the App Store launch, the two of us will sprint at full speed.

This post was written on Day 1.

It Started on the Walk Home From the Salon

You look perfect the moment you leave the hair salon. The next morning, you try to style it yourself... and something feels off.

The reason is simple: Your stylist has never seen your "everyday" hair.

Since they wash your hair before cutting, all they ever see is your hair it's been professionally styled.

And there's another problem: You can't see the back of your own head.

It's the part that people look at the most, yet

What We're Building (Working Title: HAIRLOOP)

We are building an app that lets you record a full 360° turn of your hair so you can check it from any angle and share it with your stylist (working title: HAIRLOOP).

  • : Simply sit in a chair and do one full turn.
  • : Drag with your finger to check the back of your head from any angle.
  • : Pin a note to a specific angle (e.g., "How do I style this exact part?") and ask right there.
  • : Built-in face blurring out of the box (works for public posts on Instagram or X, as well as private shares via Setlog or Messenger).

"Get advice on how to look good from every angle—without having to go to the salon."

—That is the core of this app.

The Most Interesting Discovery: "Nobody Was Complaining"

We didn't want to build based on blind assumptions, so we analyzed 1,040 posts on X (formerly Twitter).

"If the salon finish is a 10 out of 10, home reproducibility drops to a 6."

This was written by a hairstylist about their own work. The frustration was real. And yet, not a single person explicitly posted "I can't see the back or sides of my head." Normally, you'd interpret this as "there is no demand." We saw it the opposite way: "People don't complain about things they cannot see." Whether our hypothesis is right will be proven in 60 days.

If we turn out to be wrong, we promise to write "We were wrong" in a future post.

Build Rules: Keeping It As Simple As Possible

We'll leave the technical details for the next post, but here are our core development principles:

  • 36 Still Photos, Not Video: No heavy video files are kept on our servers.
  • : Just like the "360° view" on e-commerce sites, we simply swap photos smoothly.
  • : Release your finger, and it smoothly keeps rotating. That physical "tactile feel" alone is what makes people perceive it as 3D.
  • : Launch the MVP without social features.
  • : Add social features and monetization.
  • : Keep improving the UI and features based on real user feedback.
  • in the first week after launch.
  • during the competition period.

We will publish the real, raw numbers regarding these goals on September 30.

We formed a team called .

"Amaneku" comes from a Japanese word meaning "reaching every corner." We chose it to reflect our desire to build products that reach people all around the world through Shipaton.

Ryu (Business & Marketing)

2nd-year student at Kobe University (Faculty of Human Development and Environment). Member of the university entrepreneurship club, co-founder of Standy Inc. Studies applied physics and semiconductors while interning to implement AI business automation for companies. Started learning vibe coding in June. This is his very first time building an iOS app. From Saga Prefecture. In high school, attended Sol camp in Toronto, Canada, and studied in Singapore through the Tobitate! Study Abroad JAPAN program (9th high school cohort).

This article series will be updated twice a week until September 30. We will document everything as it happens, including what goes wrong. Because this is our first app, your feedback means everything to us.

items.author: Matthew Iyiola
items.content:
The acquisition has been by now, with journalists covering the angle of why the man who built Tesla spent billions on fossil fuel turbines (the answer, apparently, is to power his AI data centres). But when you visit APR Energy’s website, you meet a 403 Forbidden error; the site is inaccessible even though the servers are running.

The reasons are likely optics since there’s little upside for Elon Musk to draw attention to the acquisition or business.

Regardless of the reason, the result is that APR Energy’s website is gone, and so is everything it had built in search. For Musk, organic traffic was never going to be the point of this acquisition.

Imagine that you acquire a new business and need to take it offline while you decide how to best use its assets. Is taking the site completely offline, as Musk did with APR Energy, the right play?

No, and in this piece, I’ll share what to do instead. But first, let’s look at why taking the website down was the wrong play and which competitors stand to benefit from it.

Based on what we know, APR Energy is a company valued at $1 billion. But its organic footprint paints a much more conservative picture. See the snapshot from Ahrefs below.

    APR energy isn’t an organic powerhouse, but it has a foothold. And for businesses in this position, the play is to double down on SEO efforts: build authority, aim to rank for more keywords, and invest in BOFU content.

    On a closer look at organic visibility, we see that APR Energy ranks for two major non-branded keywords: “Genset” and “hybrid solar power plant.” Both are critical for a business in this category because they are informational keywords that can attract the right kind of audience.

    However, since being taken offline, the site has practically fallen off Google’s indexing altogether. The snapshot from Ahrefs, taken in late July, tells us that APR Energy leads the SERPs for “genset.” But on Google, it is now invisible.

    That means that these hard-earned positions are now up for grabs, and the position has been filled to satisfy searcher intent.

    The same thing is happening with the page ranking for “hybrid solar power plant": position 2 in Ahrefs, but invisible on Google.

    All the organic momentum built by the website is just gone, and that’s the real reason you can’t abruptly take a website offline. Not even to re-evaluate its business position. You’d waste all the effort and resources put into building its visibility and pave the way for the competitors.

    Ranking gaps don’t stay empty for long.

    In the SERPs screenshots, we already see competitors like Klingecorp.com taking up APR Energy’s valuable real estate.

    When sites vanish like this, the rankings typically move to fill the gap. But rankings shift all the time if a site with enough authority publishes good enough content. Based on my research, Aggreko.com is one of those sites.

    Aggreko ranks for 100X the keywords (2411 vs 20), has double the DR (69 vs 37), and nearly 50X the organic traffic (41,000 vs 850). They are perfectly poised to scoop up APR’s position.

    Interestingly, they don’t have pages dedicated to keywords like "what is a genset” or “hybrid solar power plant” at the moment, even though they cover other aspects of the topic extensively.

    A well-optimized information page targeting “genset” from a domain of that authority is an easy win. The same thing applies to every other player in this space.

    Even though APR Energy doesn’t rank for many keywords, the few they did occupy are now open. And with the right execution, that gap will be filled.

    Four ways to protect search equity after an acquisition.

    If you’re acquiring a website, here’s what to do instead of taking it down and losing all that equity.

    1. Set up a 503, not a 403

    APR Energy set up a 403, and in so doing, signaled that the entire website is inaccessible. The better move would be a 503 (Service Unavailable), which signals temporary unavailability, so crawlers return later rather than de-indexing. This way, you’re not shutting down all built-up search equity.

    2. Keep the sitemap accessible

    Even with the site down, the sitemap should remain accessible. That keeps Google aware of all the URLs on the site and sets up an uncomplicated return.

    3. Keep the top-performing pages live

    If the site needs to be taken down for reasons of optics, you can still preserve search equity by selectively leaving the top-performing pages online. In the case of APR Energy, those would be the informational blogs and service pages that rank.

    The only reason not to do this is if the team has already decided that the website has no usefulness whatsoever moving forward.

    If the website genuinely has no place in the business’s future, a savvy competitor would gladly buy it up at a reasonable price and feed it into its own organic strategy. They would migrate the performing content onto their website and redirect domains. Unlikely to happen in APR Energy’s case, but it could well be the strategy for your acquisition.

    What is the acquired website’s rankings worth?

    That’s the big question. In the case of Elon Musk, we can assume that he has no use for APR Energy’s website. It has a small organic footprint, and he can always hire SEO professionals to rebuild it if needed.

    But billionaires aren’t the only ones acquiring businesses and websites. If you find yourself in an acquisition, you can follow the four steps above (set up a 503, keep the sitemap live, leave informational pages up, or sell the websites) to keep some of the value you paid for in the website acquisition. The website is part of what you bought, and it should earn its keep.

items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
A new study argues that life may have emerged twice on Earth. "Two of the main lineages of life -- bacteria and archaea -- may have independently figured out the secrets of metabolism that upgraded them from non-living to living," reports ScienceAlert, citing a new study that "focused on the most rudimentary set of chemical reactions thought to enable this transformation." From the report: "The surprise is that the enzymes that catalyze those reactions are not conserved across the evolutionary divide that separates bacteria and archaea," says William Martin, a biologist at Heinrich Heine University Dusseldorf in Germany.
 
"The new data leave only one conclusion. The bacterial and archaeal lineages made the transition to the free-living state independently. Only free-living cells are alive. "Let's call it by name: we are looking at one origin of the genetic code, but two origins of life." That's a huge claim to make, especially when defining what life even is can be surprisingly tricky. The findings have been published in the journal Science Advances.

items.title: TimescaleDB 2.28: Faster Queries, Lighter Operations, and Better Schema Evolution
items.author: Tiger Data (creators of TimescaleDB)
items.content:
Time-series analytics at scale creates operational friction. When you're running continuous aggregates, columnar storage, and complex analytical patterns, each new metric, query pattern, and configuration tuning attempt adds complexity. Refreshes block each other, configuration changes require rebuilds, and new aggregates mean recomputing entire rollups.

Over recent , we've prioritized minimizing these hurdles by leveraging bloom filters to bypass redundant processing during high-volume operations on columnar storage. We also expanded vectorized execution across more query patterns and simplified continuous aggregate workflows by combining refresh and compression.

Now with , we're making common analytical queries faster without code changes, making continuous aggregate operations less disruptive and more flexible, and eliminating friction when evolving your schema and configuration. The result is faster queries, lighter operations, and the ability to evolve your analytics alongside your application as it scales.

Lighter, more flexible continuous aggregates:

  •  on CAggs: Add new aggregations in place without rebuilding
  • Fine-grained locking: Refreshes no longer serialize unrelated operations
  • Incremental refresh batching: Break large refreshes into batches instead of one heavy operation
  •  and : Maintenance commands now work directly on continuous aggregates

Faster queries on compressed data:

  • Metadata-driven first() and last() queries: Answer from batch metadata without decompression
  • Vectorized  expressions: Conditional logic stays on the fast path
  • Batch Sorted Merge for more queries: Lighter-weight sorting on compressed data

Better operational flexibility:

  • Sparse index retrofitting: Update configuration on existing chunks without recompression
  • Compression settings clarity: Warnings prevent misconfiguration
  • GUC for bulk loads: Skip invalidation tracking during migrations
  • Nullable  safety: Fallback to correct compression path

 PostgreSQL 15 support ends with 2.28. Plan your upgrade to PG16, PG17, or PG18.

Schema evolution: ADD COLUMN on CAggs

Schema evolution lets you add new aggregated columns without dropping and rebuilding. Before 2.28, adding a metric meant recreating the entire CAgg, recomputing all historical data (hours on large datasets), and breaking downstream consumers. Now you can  with  and backfill incrementally.

-- Add a new metric to an existing CAgg 
ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW conditions_summary_hourly 
    ADD COLUMN max_temp double precision 
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS ( 
        max(temperature) 
    ) STORED; 

-- Backfill historical data 
CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate( 
    'conditions_summary_hourly', 
    NULL, 
    NULL, 
    force => true 
);

How we made continuous aggregates operational at scale

Real-time dashboards on operational data used to force a choice: refresh frequently and block bulk loads, or refresh less often and accept stale data. Every continuous aggregate refresh acquired a table-wide lock on its materialized hypertable, blocking concurrent operations. In 2.28, we switched to row-level locking on the continuous aggregate catalog entry. Only one refresh processes a CAgg's invalidation log at a time, but the materialized table is free for concurrent operations. Refreshes and bulk loads now run in parallel.

We also made continuous aggregates more flexible.  on CAggs enables you to evolve your analytical schema in production by adding new aggregations as you learn what data you need, without downtime or rebuilds. Your dashboard design no longer locks you into upfront predictions.

-- Before 2.28: refresh acquired table-wide lock 
-- After 2.28: refresh acquires only catalog row lock 
CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate( 
    'metrics_hourly', 
    '2026-01-01', 
    '2026-02-01' 
); 
-- Other refreshes, bulk loads, and DDL can proceed

2.28 also adds two capabilities that make continuous aggregates evolve with your application:

  1. Incremental refresh batching processes large time windows in smaller batches instead of single long-running transactions. Before 2.28, refresh_continuous_aggregate() materialized the entire window atomically, holding resources and blocking vacuums. Large windows could take hours and fail mid-way. Now you can batch them.
-- Refresh a 30-day window in smaller batches 
CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate( 
    'metrics_hourly', 
    now() - INTERVAL '30 days', 
    now(), 
    options => '{ 
       "buckets_per_batch": 10, 
      "max_batches_per_execution": 20 
    }'::jsonb .
);
  1.  lets you add new aggregated columns without dropping and rebuilding. Before 2.28, adding a metric meant recreating the entire CAgg, recomputing all historical data (hours on large datasets), and breaking downstream consumers. Now you can  with  and backfill incrementally.
-- Add a new metric to an existing CAgg 
ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW conditions_summary_hourly 
    ADD COLUMN max_temp double precision 
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS ( 
      max(temperature) 
    ) STORED; 

-- Backfill historical data 
CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate( 
    'conditions_summary_hourly', 
    NULL, 
    NULL, 
    force => true 
);

 and  now work on continuous aggregates directly. Maintenance commands automatically maintain accurate planner statistics across the materialized hypertable and all its chunks, ensuring query plans stay optimal.

One of the most common queries in time-series workloads is "give me the latest value per series." Dashboards and monitoring systems run it constantly. It's a simple pattern: find the first or last value in a time range. But on compressed data, answering that query used to require decompressing entire batches just to find values that are already in the metadata. Time-sorted batches store first and last values as metadata. But before 2.28, the database decompressed anyway to answer those queries.

In 2.28, TimescaleDB extracts first(value, time) and last(value, time) aggregates directly from batch sparse indexes. No decompression. For "latest reading" queries that consume significant resources at scale, that means meaningful speedup with zero query changes. Here's what that looks like:

-- Define firstlast sparse index 
ALTER TABLE metrics SET ( 
    tsdb.index = 'firstlast(temperature)' 
); 

-- Note: Use rebuild_sparse_index() to retrofit existing chunks 
-- New chunks now answer this query from metadata alone 
SELECT 
    device_id, 
    last(temperature, time) 
FROM metrics 
WHERE time > now() - INTERVAL '7 days' 
GROUP BY device_id;

Beyond first/last, we also extended vectorized execution to cover  expressions. Before 2.28, conditional logic in aggregations forced columnar queries to fall back to row-by-row processing, making identical queries perform very differently depending on whether a  expression was present.

-- This query now stays fully vectorized 
SELECT 
    time_bucket('1 hour', ts) AS bucket, 
    SUM( 
      CASE WHEN status_code >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END 
) AS error_count, 
AVG( CASE WHEN latency_ms > 1000 THEN latency_ms END 
) AS slow_avg_latency 
FROM requests 
WHERE ts > now() - INTERVAL '7 days' 
GROUP BY bucket;

Pivot-style queries, error rate calculations, and conditional metrics all stay on the fast vectorized path. For workloads that use conditional aggregations on compressed history, that eliminates the surprise performance cliffs.

Finally, Batch Sorted Merge now applies to more query patterns.  queries on unordered compressed chunks without segmentation no longer fall back to expensive external sorts. The planner now replaces those sorts with lightweight metadata merges over pre-sorted batches.

Better operational flexibility and efficiency

Tuning time-series workloads means iterating on compression strategy. But historically, every configuration change (adding a sparse index, adjusting , optimizing ) only applied to future compressions. Existing chunks kept their old settings, creating inconsistent performance and confusion about why newly tuned queries behaved differently.

2.28 eliminates that friction.  lets you retrofit sparse index configuration to existing chunks without recompressing. Sparse indexes are metadata. Updating them shouldn't require rewriting data. Below is the actual code snippet you can leverage:

-- Change sparse index settings on the hypertable 
ALTER TABLE metrics SET ( 
    tsdb.index = 'minmax(value)' 
); 

-- Retrofit existing chunks without recompression 
SELECT _timescaledb_functions.rebuild_sparse_index( 
    '_timescaledb_internal._hyper_1_42_chunk' 
);

Compression settings changes now emit warnings clarifying that new settings apply only to future compressions. This closes the gap: users assume  sets configuration across the entire dataset, but it only affects new chunks.

For correctness, nullable ORDER BY columns now safely fall back to decompress-compress during recompression, preventing silent incorrect results when min/max metadata doesn't account for s.

Gapfill row count estimation improved so  queries get more accurate planner statistics and better query plans.

For bulk migrations, a new GUC timescaledb.skip_cagg_invalidation suppresses continuous aggregate invalidation tracking during bulk loads. Migration tools no longer generate useless invalidation entries that trigger expensive refresh storms.

PostgreSQL 15: Final Release and Migration Path

PostgreSQL 15 support ends with TimescaleDB 2.28. Going forward, only PostgreSQL 16, 17, and 18 are supported.

If you're on PG15, plan your upgrade to PG17 or PG18 now. We'll begin upgrading instances in production the week of September 15th, so you should plan your migration path over the next two months to avoid downtime. Postgres upgrades are typically non-disruptive (seconds to minutes of downtime using logical replication or physical backup/restore), and newer Postgres versions bring improvements in query parallelism, vector search optimization, and compression.

For workloads running continuous aggregates at scale, columnar queries with conditional logic, or iterating on compression configuration, 2.28 removes operational friction: refreshes don't serialize, queries stay vectorized, and tuning doesn't require rewrites.

items.title: OAC Technology Builds Its Reputation On Tailored IT Support And Real Human Service
items.author: Sanya Kapoor
items.content:
*Photo Courtesy of OAC Technology \ *

A technician who already knows a client's network configuration can fix a problem in minutes. A technician meeting that same network for the first time, mid-crisis, needs to ask questions before they can even start. That gap, between familiarity and a cold start, is where says its reputation actually gets built, one account at a time, rather than through any single campaign.

The Handoff Most Providers Never Explain

Most managed IT providers describe their support as personal without explaining what that means operationally. OAC Technology's version has a specific mechanism behind it: according to the company's own service description, clients work with the same IT professional roughly 90 percent of the time, a dedicated technician assigned to the account rather than pulled from a general pool as tickets arrive. That technician accumulates account-specific knowledge over months and years, the kind of context that turns a ten-minute diagnosis into a two-minute one simply because the person on the call already knows what the last three problems were.

The harder operational question is what happens when that primary technician is unavailable. OAC states that in those cases, a second, equally qualified technician has access to the client's records and can pick up the account where the first left off, rather than starting the relationship over. That detail matters more than it might first appear. Continuity built entirely around one irreplaceable person is fragile; continuity backed by documented account history that a second technician can actually use is closer to a real system than a lucky pairing.

What Tailored Support Looks Like In Practice

OAC Technology describes itself on its website as operating on a first name basis with clients, a line that could read as a slogan if the company did not also describe the infrastructure behind it. Clients are matched with a technician based on the specific needs of their business rather than assigned arbitrarily, and that matching is meant to hold for the life of the relationship rather than resetting with each new support request.

That structure shows up in independent client reviews as well, where customers describe working repeatedly with specific named technicians rather than a rotating, anonymous help desk. Reviewers cite fast turnaround on printer and software configuration issues, patient troubleshooting on non-technical problems like data recovery from a damaged drive, and a consistent point of contact across multiple service requests over time. That pattern, the same names appearing across unrelated reviews months apart, is a rough proxy for whether a continuity model is actually functioning as described rather than existing only in marketing copy.

Reputation Built Without A Marketing Department

OAC Technology has grown for more than two decades largely on referrals rather than an outbound sales function, and a tailored, name-based support model is the kind of thing that produces referrals specifically because it is hard to fake at scale. A client recommending a provider to a colleague is usually not citing SOC 2 compliance or service tier structure. They are citing the fact that their technician picked up the phone and already knew what was wrong.

That word-of-mouth pattern has limits worth naming honestly. It depends on technician retention; if OAC's staff turned over quickly, the continuity model would collapse regardless of how it is designed on paper. It also depends on the account load staying manageable enough that a dedicated technician can actually retain the account-specific knowledge the model relies on. Neither the company nor any outside source has published turnover or caseload figures, so those remain reasonable questions rather than settled ones.

What can be said with more confidence is that the underlying mechanism, a real technician-continuity structure with a documented handoff plan, is a more specific claim than most competitors make, and specificity is usually the harder thing to manufacture. Any provider can write "we care about our clients" on a homepage. Building a system where a second technician can actually pick up an account cold, using another person's notes, and still resolve the issue without the client noticing the switch, requires documentation discipline that most small providers do not bother maintaining because it takes ongoing effort with no immediate payoff.

That is arguably the more honest way to evaluate a reputation claim like this one. Not by asking whether a company says it values relationships, since every competitor says that, but by asking what specific operational choice would break if the claim were false. For OAC Technology, the answer is the handoff mechanism itself. A company that talks about personal service but has no real continuity system usually reveals it the moment a client's regular contact goes on vacation. OAC's structure is built, at least as described, to survive exactly that moment.

SOAX is the precision instrument of this group, and carrier-level targeting at this price is rare. It suits quality-sensitive collection in awkward geographies. The limitations: a hard $90 entry with no pay-as-you-go, traffic that does not roll over, and a datacenter pool that is US-only.

5. Proxyrack: unmetered bandwidth on a thread-priced model

Proxyrack is one of the longer-running names in the proxy market and prices differently from everyone else here. Instead of paying per gigabyte, you buy concurrent threads and run unmetered traffic across them, which changes the economics of bandwidth-hungry jobs.

Proxyrack states 5M+ rotating Residential IPs across 140+ countries, a 20,000+ Datacenter pool, and Mobile endpoints in 70+ countries. Third-party sources cite anything from 2M to 85M, so treat the pool figure as soft.

•    Residential (premium, private, unlimited), Datacenter (USA rotating, global rotating, static USA), and Mobile Proxies. Static USA covers the persistent-IP case others sell as ISP Proxies.

•    country, city, and ISP.

•    HTTP, SOCKS, and UDP – broader than most of this list – with rotating and sticky ports and custom rotation timers.

•    plans start at $49.95/month, with unmetered tiers priced per concurrent thread rather than per GB. A 3-day trial of the full product suite costs $13.95.

•    not publicly disclosed. Independent testers report figures, but Proxyrack publishes none of its own.

email and a public forum. No live chat, and no dedicated account management.

•    web scraper API, Android SDK, sub-users, and a 3-day money-back guarantee.

Proxyrack earns its place when bandwidth, not requests, is your cost driver – heavy media or full-page collection where per-GB billing gets punishing. The limitations are significant: pricing is hard to compare against per-GB competitors, support is email-only, and the inconsistent pool figures mean you should trial first.

6. Webshare: the cheapest way in

Webshare is a self-serve platform built around a genuinely usable free plan and low entry pricing. It suits individual developers and small teams who want proxies working in ten minutes without a sales conversation.

•    80M+ Residential IPs across 195 countries.

•    Residential, Datacenter, and ISP Proxies. No Mobile Proxies in the lineup.

•    country, state, and city. No ASN or carrier targeting.

•    HTTP(S) and SOCKS5, with rotating and static options.

•    Datacenter Proxy servers from $2.99/month for 100 proxies, ISP from $0.30 per proxy, rotating Residential around $3.50/GB. Bandwidth is consumed within the billing month.

•    no headline success rate published, which is a gap given how central reliability is to the decision.

•    self-serve, with no SLA or dedicated account manager even on paid plans.

a permanent free plan of 10 proxies and 1GB per month with no card required, Chrome and Firefox browser extensions, and an API for pulling a proxy list.

Webshare is the right first purchase for a solo developer or a proof of concept, and the free plan is real rather than decorative. The limitations follow from the price: no mobile proxies, no ASN targeting, no published performance figures, and support that assumes you can solve your own problems.

7. IPRoyal: affordable coverage with traffic that never expires

IPRoyal's defining feature is billing rather than pool size: bandwidth you buy stays available until you use it. That matters more than it sounds for teams running scraping projects in bursts rather than continuously.

32M+ Residential IPs across 195 countries.

•    Residential, Datacenter, ISP, and Mobile proxies.

country, state, and city. No ASN or carrier filtering.

•    Supported protocols: HTTP(S) and SOCKS5, with sticky sessions up to seven days – the longest window here.

•    pay-as-you-go Residential starts around $7/GB and drops toward $1.75/GB at volume. Traffic does not expire and there is no minimum subscription.

no verified success rate is published; third-party tests place it mid-table.

24/7 chat, well reviewed for a provider at this price point.

•    browser extensions, unlimited concurrent sessions with no per-session fee, and a higher-grade pool for harder targets.

IPRoyal is the pick for intermittent work where a monthly allowance would go to waste, and seven-day sticky sessions are genuinely useful for multi-step flows. The limitations: a 32M pool is small once you push concurrency, there is no free trial, and the entry per-GB rate is steep until you commit to volume.

8. Rayobyte: datacenter-first and developer-friendly

Rayobyte, formerly Blazing SEO, is a US-based provider that grew out of a datacenter specialism and added Residential later. It suits SEO tooling, rank tracking, and high-volume collection against targets that do not require Residential IP addresses.

•    Network: 300K+ Datacenter IPs across roughly 27 countries. The Residential pool size is not consistently disclosed – third-party estimates run from 30M to over 100M, which is itself a reason to test rather than trust the figure.

•    Proxy types: Residential, Datacenter, ISP, and Mobile proxies.

•    Targeting: country and city, with city-level coverage strongest inside the US and thinner elsewhere.

•    Supported protocols: HTTP, HTTPS, and SOCKS5 on Datacenter and ISP; SOCKS5 on Residential is limited. Sticky sessions run from 1 to 120 minutes.

•    Pricing: Datacenter from around $1/IP with unlimited bandwidth, ISP per IP, and Residential entry around $1/GB – though rotating tiers price considerably higher. Some Residential packages are one-time purchases that do not expire.

•    Performance: no headline success rate published by the provider.

•    Support: US-based and well reviewed for handling integration questions.

•    Other features: automatic dead-proxy replacement, a published sourcing policy, and a scraping API.

Our take: Rayobyte is a strong datacenter shop with an unusually transparent ethics stance, which helps when procurement asks where the IPs came from. Two limitations: Residential is the weaker half of the portfolio, and the gap between the advertised entry rate and the realistic rotating rate is wide enough to catch buyers out.

9. DataImpulse: the lowest cost per GB

DataImpulse owns its IPs directly rather than reselling another network, and prices accordingly. It is built for teams whose main selection criterion is cost per successful request at volume, with a deliberately lean feature set.

•    90M+ Residential IPs across 195 countries, first-party owned.

Residential, Datacenter, and Mobile proxies. No ISP Proxies in the lineup.

country, city, ASN, and ZIP, with no add-on fee – unusual at this price.

•    HTTP, HTTPS, and SOCKS5, with UDP on request. Rotation is per request by default, with sticky sessions up to 120 minutes.

•    $1/GB Residential, falling to roughly $0.70–$0.80/GB in bulk; Datacenter from $0.50/GB; Mobile from $2/GB. Entry is $5 for 5GB, with no subscription and no traffic expiry.

•    99.9% uptime claimed by the provider; independent verification is thin.

•    24/7 human support, rare at the bottom of the price range.

real-time usage dashboard and pay-as-you-go billing, no minimum commitment.

DataImpulse is the cheapest credible per-GB rate here, and ZIP-level targeting at $1/GB is a genuine outlier. It suits large batch jobs where you control the scheduler and can absorb a retry. The limitation is breadth: no ISP Proxies, no advanced tooling, and a community small enough that you will be reading docs rather than forums.

10. Infatica: a balanced budget-to-mid option

Infatica sells all four proxy types plus scraper tooling and leans on compliance positioning, including a business-use-only acceptable use policy. It fits brand protection, ad verification, and agencies reselling under their own name.

Infatica's Residential page headlines 35M+ IPs, but other pages and third-party reviews cite anything from 10M to 60M. Coverage spans 150+ countries.

Residential, Datacenter, ISP, and Mobile Proxies.

•    Targeting: country and city on Residential, country on mobile. City depth is uneven outside major markets, so verify availability first.

•    HTTP(S) and SOCKS5, with some protocol limits on mobile plans.

Residential entry sits around $8/GB on the smallest plan, falling toward roughly $1/GB at very high volume. Datacenter starts near $1/IP. Paid trial only, no free plan.

not publicly disclosed.

•    responsive on configuration and scaling questions, with sub-user management and usage reporting.

white-label reselling for agencies, a scraper API, and ISO certification.

Our take: Infatica is a reasonable all-rounder if you want every proxy type from one vendor and value the compliance framing during procurement. Two limitations stand out: the pool figure is the least consistent here, and the entry price is high for a provider positioned as budget-friendly – the attractive rates appear only at volumes most buyers will not reach.

Choosing the right proxy for web scraping

Ten options is more than anyone needs. What you need is a rule for picking, so work through these four questions in order.

Match the proxy type to the target first. This decision does more for your success rate than the choice of vendor.

Bulk collection, public catalogues, sitemaps

Rotating Residential Proxies

Marketplaces, search engines, listings

ISP Proxies or static Residential Proxies

Logins, carts, multi-step flows

Mobile-first apps and social platforms

Use rotating proxies to distribute requests across many IPs for general web scraping. Use static Residential Proxies or sticky sessions whenever a session must keep the same IP address – logins, carts, and multi-step flows fall apart if the exit IP changes mid-journey. Most providers let you set the rotation interval, so this is a per-endpoint choice, not a per-account one.

. Request volume, concurrency, and average page weight decide whether bandwidth based pricing or per-IP pricing is cheaper. Back of an envelope: a browser-rendered page pulls roughly 1–3MB, so 1GB buys 300–1,000 pages. A raw HTTP request against a JSON endpoint might be 50KB, so the same gigabyte buys 20,000. If you run headless browsers, model 2× your first estimate. Above a few hundred gigabytes a month, per-IP or per-thread plans usually win.

Do the budget reality check. Free proxies and cheap shared proxies look like savings until you price a failed request. A pool at $1/GB with a 90% success rate costs more per usable page than one at $3/GB and 99.5%, once you count retries, CAPTCHA managing, and engineering time. Dedicated proxies earn their keep when a single flagged IP would interrupt a business process rather than just a job.

Do not blame the proxy for everything. User agents, request headers, TLS fingerprints, and rate limits matter as much as proxy rotation. A good proxy service will not rescue a scraper pulling 40 pages a second from one session with a default Python user agent. Fix the client first, then buy the pool.

Three shortlists. Enterprise teams scraping protected sites at volume should start with , with Bright Data as the alternative if you need datasets and a scraping browser in the same contract. Mid-market teams get the best price-to-quality from Decodo, with SOAX close behind when targeting precision beats speed. Budget buyers should look at Webshare's free plan for a first project, DataImpulse for the lowest cost per GB, and IPRoyal when non-expiring traffic is worth more than a lower headline rate.

Whichever way you lean, run a trial against your own target before committing. The best proxy for web scraping is the one that clears your site at your volume – and that is a ten-minute test, not a purchasing decision.

Frequently asked questions

What type of proxy is best for web scraping?

There is no single answer – it depends on the target. Choose Datacenter Proxies for high-volume collection against sites with light defenses, where speed and cost win. Choose Residential Proxies when you need Residential IP addresses that look like ordinary users on most websites. Choose ISP Proxies for Residential trust at Datacenter speed with a static IP. Choose mobile proxies for mobile-first platforms, the hardest and most expensive targets. Many teams run two pools and route requests by target.

Are free proxies safe for web scraping?

Not for anything that matters. Free proxies are shared among multiple users, frequently already flagged by the sites you want to reach, and often unencrypted. Whoever runs the server can log or modify traffic passing through it, so anything touching credentials is a real risk. They are fine for a one-off connectivity test and unsuitable for production or anything where the data has value. Most paid providers offer a free plan or cheap trial that removes the reason to use them.

How many proxies do you need for web scraping?

It depends on request volume, the target's rate limits, and how aggressively that particular site restricts repeat visitors. A rough rule for a static proxy list is one IP per one to two requests per minute you intend to sustain, then adjust on your error rate. With rotating Residential proxies the maths changes entirely: you buy bandwidth rather than a proxy list, the provider handles proxy rotation, and the planning question becomes gigabytes per month.

Can you still be turned away when using proxies?

Yes. Proxies solve the IP address problem and nothing else. Browser fingerprinting, mismatched headers and user agents, predictable timing, and Residential IPs other customers have already burned on your target will all get requests refused. The usual next fixes are JavaScript rendering, CAPTCHA handling, realistic header sets, and slower pacing. If your success rate collapses on one particular site but holds everywhere else, the proxy pool is rarely the cause.
